title: About
text:
Data Insights is a collection of hands-on R tutorials — from the basics of pipes and functions to data wrangling with the tidyverse and statistics like t-tests and effect sizes.
Written by djani.

text:
Aufgabe 2 – Kenngrößen
Berechnen Sie Mittelwert, Median und Standardabweichung für die Variable „Kaffeekonsum“ über die gesamte Stichprobe.

# als tabelle 
kaffee |> 
  summarise(mean   = mean(kaffeekonsum),
            median = median(kaffeekonsum),
            sd     = sd(kaffeekonsum))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>    mean median    sd
#>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1  3.33   3.37 0.849

Berechnen Sie Mittelwerte, Mediane und Standardabweichungen für die Variable „Konzentrationsfähigkeit“ getrennt nach den beiden Gruppen.

kaffee |> 
  group_by(gruppe) |> 
  summarise(mean   = mean(kaffeekonsum),
            median = median(kaffeekonsum),
            sd     = sd(kaffeekonsum))

#>   <chr>          <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 entkoffeiniert  3.36   3.36 0.982

Aufgabe 3 – Visualisierung
Stellen Sie die Daten für die Variable „Kaffeekonsum“ über die gesamte Stichprobe in einem Histogramm mit geeigneter Klassenzahl (Ermittlung über Faustformel aus der Vorlesung) dar.

  ggplot(kaffee, aes(x = kaffeekonsum)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = bin) +
  labs(

    x = "Kaffeekonsum",
    y = "Häufigkeit"

  theme_minimal()

hh

title: t-test
text:
Eleonore arbeitet weiterhin als studentische Hilfskraft in dem Projekt zu Depression unter jungen Menschen an der Kinder- und Jugendpsychatrie. Sie hatte schon den Datensatz studie_4_depression.csv zur Analyse vorbereitet. Nun wurde diese Studie repliziert und Eleonore soll diese Daten nun auch zur Analyse vorbereiten und erste Analysen durchführen. Eleonore importiert die Daten, führt die gleichen Vorverarbeitungsschritte durch (d.h., z-Transformation anhand der Mittelwerte und Standardabweichungen der jeweiligen Erhebungsinstrumente), und schaut sich die Verteilungen der Daten an.

library(tidyverse)
df <- read_csv2("Daten_Uebung_6.csv")

In der ersten Analysen soll Eleonore testen, ob sich die Mittelwerte der jeweiligen untersuchten Populationen vom entsprechenden Skalenmittelwert unterscheiden. Dafür kann sie direkt die z-transformierten Werte verwenden, denn durch die z-Transformation ist der entsprechende Skalenmittelwert in allen drei Altersgruppen mu = 0 und die einzelnen Werte zeigen direkt die standardisierte Abweichung von diesem Mittelwert. Damit schätzt der jeweilige Mittelwert der z-transformierten Werte direkt die mittlere Abweichung der untersuchten Populationen vom entsprechenden Skalenmittelwert.

df |> 
  group_by(questionnaire) |> 
  summarise(
    m  = mean(index_z),
    se = sd(index)/sqrt(n())
  )



t.test(
  Dresden %>%
    pull(Zufriedenheit_eigene_Seite),
  mu = 18,
  alternative = ”two.sided”)


df <- 
  janitor::clean_names(df)

eigene_seite <- 
  df |> 
  pull(zufriedenheit_eigene_seite)

eigene_seite

title: Vectors
text:
In R, a vector is the most basic and essential data structure. It’s simply a sequence of elements—like a list of numbers, characters, or logical values—all of the same type.
You can think of a vector like a row of boxes, where each box holds one value—and all boxes must hold the same kind of thing.

x <- 1:3
x
#> [1] 1 2 3

title: Vectors
text:
🆎 Types of Vectors
There are many data types. You can use function class() to see the type. Here are the main ones:








Data Type
Code Example
Description




Numeric
x <- 3.14
A real (floating point) number. Used for quantities with fractions like weight, height, gpa score. Pretty much most common.


Integer
x <- 5L
Similar to Numeric but used for discrete counts . Number of people, apples, floors in a building.


Character
x <- "hello"
A text (string) value. Names, comment


Logical
x <- TRUE
Also called Boolean value: TRUE or FALSE . Used when there are only two states for something, yin/yan, dead/alive, pass/fail, on/off, keep/discard.


Date
x <- as.Date("2020-02-01")
date format. you can do math operations like this then as.Date("2020-01-02") - as.Date("2020-01-01")

title: Vectors
text:
📦 Example
Lets create some vectors of different types and then combine them together into a data.frame .

🔤 Character vector:

name <- c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "Olivia", "Max")
gender <- c("female", "male", "diverse", "female", "male")
class(name)
#> [1] "character"



📊 Numeric vector:

height <- c(1.71, 1.82, 1.78, 1.68, 1.95)
weight <- c(56, 80, 75, 54, 95)

class(height)
#> [1] "numeric"



✅ Logical vector:

is_married <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)
class(is_married)
#> [1] "logical"

# kleiner exkurs
# why logical vectors are useful
# the square brackets '[' are used to select elements of a vector
name[1]
#> [1] "Alice"
name[3]
#> [1] "Charlie"
# vorsicht
name[99]
#> [1] NA

# instead of numbers we can pass a logical vector with the same length
# which will keep elements TRUE
name[is_married]
#> [1] "Alice"   "Charlie"




📅 Date vector:

# i will generate 5 random birthdays 

# all are born in the year 2000
beginning <- as.Date("2000-01-01")
end       <- as.Date("2000-12-31")

class(beginning)
#> [1] "Date"

# arithmetics is possible
end - beginning
#> Time difference of 365 days


# generate all dates in 2000
# and pick 5 at random
# (i am using the new pipe symbol '|>')
birthday <- 
  seq(from = beginning, to = end, by = 1) |>  
  sample(5)

birthday
#> [1] "2000-04-20" "2000-07-04" "2000-02-27" "2000-02-01" "2000-03-11"

# same thing without piping
  # option 1. with an intermediate object for all 2000 dates
x <- seq(beginning, end, by = 1)
birthday <- sample(x, 5)

length(x)
#> [1] 366
head(x)
#> [1] "2000-01-01" "2000-01-02" "2000-01-03" "2000-01-04" "2000-01-05"
#> [6] "2000-01-06"
tail(x)
#> [1] "2000-12-26" "2000-12-27" "2000-12-28" "2000-12-29" "2000-12-30"
#> [6] "2000-12-31"

  # option 2. nested, e.g. without intermediate x
birthday <- sample(seq(beginning, end, by = 1), 5)

title: Effect Size and Cohen’s d
text:
Imagine we are studying the effect of a new anti-ADHD medication on patient’s ability to focus. We design a controlled experiment and measure the focus time of individuals with and without the drug.

library(tidyverse)

# focus time in min 
placebo   <- c(15, 16, 13, 15, 14, 16, 16, 17 , 13, 15, 14)
treatment <- c(19, 19, 16, 18, 18, 17, 19, 18 , 18, 16, 16)

# mean time 
mean_placebo    <- mean(placebo)
mean_treatment  <- mean(treatment)

# standard deviations
sd_placebo   <- sd(placebo)
sd_treatment <- sd(treatment)

pooled_sd <- (sd_placebo + sd_treatment)/2

Now we have a fictitious experiment where it seems that the drug leads to increase of focus time.

# for visualisation only
df <- 
  data.frame(
    mean = c(mean_placebo, mean_treatment),
    sd   = c(sd_placebo, sd_treatment)
  ) 

rownames(df) <- c("placebo", "treatment")

# focus time
df
#>               mean       sd
#> placebo   14.90909 1.300350
#> treatment 17.63636 1.206045

title: Effect Size and Cohen’s d
text:
Imagine we are studying the effect of a new anti-ADHD medication on patient’s ability to focus. We design a controlled experiment and measure the focus time of individuals with and without the drug.

library(tidyverse)

# focus time in min 
placebo   <- c(15, 16, 13, 15, 14, 16, 16, 17 , 13, 15, 14)
treatment <- c(19, 19, 16, 18, 18, 17, 19, 18 , 18, 16, 16)

# mean time 
mean_placebo    <- mean(placebo)
mean_treatment  <- mean(treatment)

# standard deviations
sd_placebo   <- sd(placebo)
sd_treatment <- sd(treatment)

pooled_sd <- (sd_placebo + sd_treatment)/2

Now we have a fictitious experiment where it seems that the drug leads to increase of focus time.

# for visualisation only
df <- 
  data.frame(
    mean = c(mean_placebo, mean_treatment),
    sd   = c(sd_placebo, sd_treatment)
  ) 

rownames(df) <- c("placebo", "treatment")

# focus time
df
#>               mean       sd
#> placebo   14.90909 1.300350
#> treatment 17.63636 1.206045

title: Effect Size and Cohen’s d
text:
Statistical significance
Lets see if the increase between placebo and the treatment is statistically significant assuming p < 0.05.

t.test(treatment, placebo, "greater")
#> 
#>  Welch Two Sample t-test
#> 
#> data:  treatment and placebo
#> t = 5.1002, df = 19.888, p-value = 2.777e-05
#> alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is greater than 0
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  1.804738      Inf
#> sample estimates:
#> mean of x mean of y 
#>  17.63636  14.90909

Yes the diff(c(mean_placebo, mean_treatment)) is around 3 minutes and is statistically significant because there is a miniscule (only p = 0.0028 %) chance that those two sets (placebo and treatment) stem from the same underlying population. In other words there is only a very small chance that the treatment and placebo have the same mean value.
But what about the effect?

title: Effect Size and Cohen’s d
text:
Effect size using Cohen’s d

Theory
The effect size shows how much the treatment affects the people. How big is the change. The formulation of effect size is
\[
d = \frac{M_{\text{med}} - M_{\text{placebo}}}{s_{\text{pooled}}}
\]
If the difference in the nominator would be equal the standard deviation (\(M_{med} - M_{placebo} = s_{pooled}\) ) then \(d = \frac{s_{pooled}}{s_{pooled}} = 1\) and we woud say that on average the treatment leads to one standard deviation increase in effect. In literature 0.2 is weak effect, 0.6 is a moderate effect, and everything above 0.8 standard deviations is a very strong effect.
Lets calculate \(d\) for our fictitious example.

d <- (mean_treatment - mean_placebo)/pooled_sd
d
#> [1] 2.176251

# using function in
library(lsr)
cohensD(treatment, placebo)
#> [1] 2.174713



Interpretation
The effect of this drug is 2.175 times the pooled standard deviation of the study group - a very strong effect on focus time. On average, the drug leads to an increase in focus time by about (d x pooled_sd) 2.725 minutes.
So while statistical significance tells us that we can be sure that the numbers are trully different and not just a random realization of the same underlying process (or population), the effect size informs us about the magnitude of the difference.

title: Pipes
text:
The pipe %>% was introduced with the tidyverse dialect back around 2015. Because it was borrowed from another library called magrittr you will often see that name too. The pipe made the code more human readable. It was so revolutionary that the R-consortium decided to introduce its own version into the standard base R dialect as |> .
The two pipe operators have very similar behavior with one considerable difference - magrittr uses . as a placeholder to explicate the destination whereas base pipe uses _ (underscore) as a placeholder.

library(tidyverse)

# magrittr pipe
1:5 %>% sum()
#> [1] 15

# base R pipe
1:5 |> sum()
#> [1] 15

# with placeholder in magrittr
1:5 %>% sum(.) 
#> [1] 15

# with placeholder in base R
1:5 |> sum(... = _)
#> [1] 15

title: Pipes
text:
The pipe %>% was introduced with the tidyverse dialect back around 2015. Because it was borrowed from another library called magrittr you will often see that name too. The pipe made the code more human readable. It was so revolutionary that the R-consortium decided to introduce its own version into the standard base R dialect as |> .
The two pipe operators have very similar behavior with one considerable difference - magrittr uses . as a placeholder to explicate the destination whereas base pipe uses _ (underscore) as a placeholder.

library(tidyverse)

# magrittr pipe
1:5 %>% sum()
#> [1] 15

# base R pipe
1:5 |> sum()
#> [1] 15

# with placeholder in magrittr
1:5 %>% sum(.) 
#> [1] 15

# with placeholder in base R
1:5 |> sum(... = _)
#> [1] 15

title: Pipes
text:
How does it work?
The pipe takes the object on its left side and brings it (pipes it) into the function on its right side. By default it pipes it to the first position in the function. Using the . placeholder (_ for base), we can explicitly send the object to a specific location in the function.

# basic idea
a |> f()
# is equivalent to
f(a)

a |> f(b)
# is equivalent to
f(a, b)

# with `.` placeholder for magrittr
a %>% f(b, .)
# is equivalent to 
f(b, a)

# with `_` placeholder for base r
a |> (b, _)
# is equivalent to 
f(b, a)

title: Pipes
text:
Examples
The power of the pipe becomes apparent when we have a long sequence of consecutive operations each taking the result of the previous one. In this case we are not interested in the intermediate results, but rather in the final result.

x <- c(1, 4, 9, 16, 25)

# long sequence of operation
x |>
  sqrt() |>
  log() |>
  round(digits = 2) |>
  sort(decreasing = TRUE)
#> [1] 1.61 1.39 1.10 0.69 0.00

# equivalent to 
x2 <- sqrt(x)
x3 <- log(x2)
x4 <- round(x3, digits = 2)
sort(x4, decreasing = TRUE)
#> [1] 1.61 1.39 1.10 0.69 0.00


# example 2 - cleaning vector of words
sentences <- c(" Hello ", "world! ", "  How ", "are", " you? ")
sentences
#> [1] " Hello " "world! " "  How "  "are"     " you? "
length(sentences)
#> [1] 5


cleaned <- 
  sentences |>
  trimws() |>                           # Remove leading/trailing spaces
  tolower() |>                          # Convert to lower case
  gsub("[[:punct:]]", "", x = _) |>     # Remove punctuation
  paste(collapse = " ")                 # Collapse to a single string

cleaned
#> [1] "hello world how are you"
length(cleaned)
#> [1] 1

text:
R is not just a tool—it’s a language. Just as any language it has:

Vocabulary (functions, objects)
Syntax (rules of structure)
Grammar (how elements combine)

Lets learn more about the grammar of functions.

title: Functions
text:
🗣️ Functions = Verbs
Functions perform actions. Most functions expect input (arguments) and return a result. Think of functions as transformer, they take something in and transform it into something else.

Here is a more formal representation:

Does this remind you of something? The pipe synthax looks very similar. In fact, we can use a rechtsrum (->) assignment operator to write an expression exactly like this: a |> f() -> b

# example 
a <- 1:5

a |> mean() -> b
b
#> [1] 3
# yes you can use `->` assignment too :) 

# same as 
b <- mean(a)
b
#> [1] 3

title: Functions
text:
🤖 Transformers vs. Reducers
As I said, functions are transformers, they transform the input vector (a) into something else (b). Strictly speaking, transformers will keep the length of vectors a and b the same (length(a) == length(b)). Reducers on the other hand will squish (reduce) the length of the input vector down to (normally) 1 element. For example, summary functions like sum(), min(), max(), sd() are reducers. They reduce the information from the vector to a single value.

# example
a <- 1:5

# transformer: a hoch 2
b <- a^2
b
#> [1]  1  4  9 16 25
length(a) == length(b)
#> [1] TRUE

# reducer
c <- max(a)
c
#> [1] 5
length(a) == length(c)
#> [1] FALSE

title: Functions
text:
🔤 Arguments
The general form of a function consist of function_name(arguments) Commonly, the first argument (often named x) is the most important and is the data (vector) which will be transformed. and the other arguments describe “how” it will be transformed.


# vector with missing values (NA = not available)
a <- c(1:100, NA, NA, NA)
tail(a)
#> [1]  98  99 100  NA  NA  NA

# NA will always propagate forward !!!
sd(a)
#> [1] NA

# remove NA
sd(a, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 29.01149

# use 
help(mean)
# to find out about all available options in a function
